rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - Polarising power ∝ charge² / radius (ionic potential φ = z/r) - Coulomb energy ∝ |q₁q₂| / r (lattice attraction basis) - Li⁺ 76 pm < Na⁺ 102 pm < K⁺ 138 pm (polarising ladder)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Formula unit ≠ molecule:** NaCl is a formula unit of an infinite lattice, not a discrete molecule — "molecule of NaCl" is a mark-losing phrase.  ·  **Polarisation direction:** the cation polarises (distorts) the anion — small/high-charge cation pulls, large anion is pulled.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***LiCl dissolves in ethanol and acetone where NaCl barely does*** — the observable fingerprint of Li⁺'s stronger polarisation of Cl⁻.

rows.text: Fajan: "small cation, big anion, big charges, 18-e⁻ cation → covalent." Conductivity: "solid no, molten yes." Lattice ladder: MgO > CaO > NaCl > KCl in mp.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Every ionic bond has some covalent character (Fajan's polarisation); every covalent bond has some ionic character (polarity). The 100% pure bond is a limiting idealisation — the ionic–covalent picture is a continuum.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Ionic bond = electrostatic attraction between ions formed by electron transfer (metal low IE + non-metal high EA + high lattice energy). Properties: hard brittle crystals, high mp/bp, conduct only when molten/aqueous, soluble in polar solvents, fast ionic reactions.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Magnesium oxide's melting point (2852 °C) is so high that MgO lines furnaces — doubly charged, small ions build the strongest common lattice.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Bond of Full Transfer When the electronegativity gap is a canyon — metal meets non-metal — electrons are not shared but **surrendered**. Sodium hands its 3s electron to chlorine; the resulting Na⁺ and Cl⁻ lock into a three-dimensional lattice by sheer electrostatic attraction. That attraction **is** the ionic (electrovalent) bond.…  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Formation mechanism - **Electron transfer:** metal atoms (low IE) lose electrons → cations; non-metal atoms (high EA) gain them → anions. - Na (2,8,1) → Na⁺ (2,8) + e⁻; Cl (2,8,7) + e⁻ → Cl⁻ (2,8,8). Both reach noble-gas configurations.…  ·  ## 3. rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ## 6. Common Confusions **Ionic bond is not directional:** an Na⁺ attracts every neighbouring Cl⁻ equally — the "bond" is the whole lattice's attraction, not a pair-specific link. That is why formula units (NaCl) are not molecules.  ·  **Covalent character in ionic bonds is normal, not anomalous:** Fajan's rules mean every "ionic" compound has some electron distortion; 100% ionic exists only as an idealisation.  ·  **Solid ionic compounds do not conduct:** conduction requires mobile charge carriers; in the solid the ions are locked in place — the common exam trap.

How do they explain the covalent character of LiCl vs NaCl?** — Covalent character increases with small cation size, large anion size, high ionic charges and cations of 18-electron configuration.…  ·  **NEB-style (2m): Why is MgO's melting point (2852 °C) far higher than NaCl's (801 °C)?** — Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ carry double the charge of Na⁺/Cl⁻ and are smaller, so the electrostatic attraction (and lattice energy, ≈ −3795 kJ mol⁻¹) is far greater — more energy is needed to disrupt the lattice.
